newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Presidential challenger leads in Moldovan vote.
newsitem.headline: Presidential challenger leads in Moldovan vote.

text.p: Left-wing challenger Petru Lucinschi had a clear lead over Moldovan President Mircea Snegur in early counting for the former Soviet republic's first presidential election run-off on Sunday.

After a bitter campaign that pitted the president against the government and culminated with Lucinschi, the chairman of parliament, accusing Snegur of plotting to rig the vote, the challenger had an 11-point lead with 12.46 percent counted.

Pro-Snegur students gathered in front of the electoral commission in the centre of the capital, Chisinau, vowing to protest if the president lost. But they numbered only about 100 and armed police said they expected no trouble.
Electoral commission chairman Petru Railean told Reuters Lucinschi had 55.66 percent of the vote to Snegur's 44.34.

The count had yet to start in Chisinau, where Lucinschi is expected to do well among Moldova's mainly urban one-third Russian-speaking minority, who are suspicious of Snegur's calls for closer ties with the majority's ethnic kin in Romania.
Turnout an hour before polls closed was 68.5 percent, up on the 67 percent first-round total on November 17.
Railean said there were no significant violations of voting rules. Foreign observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe also had no reports of major trouble.

OSCE coordinator Kare Vollan told Reuters his observers had paid particular attention to polling stations close to the Russian-speaking Dnestr region, which broke away in 1990 fearing Moldovans wanted to unite with Romania.

Authorities in the 700,000-strong area, where hundreds died in fighting in 1992, boycotted the poll but said local people could vote elsewhere. Only a few thousand did so in the first round when the OSCE reported some incidents with Dnestr forces.
Pledging to press on with incomplete western-style market reforms, the 56-year-old Snegur polled 39 percent in the first round and has since been endorsed by pro-Romanian nationalists.

But he faced stiff opposition from within the ranks of the state. Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, knocked out in the first round supported Lucinschi, who was also backed by communists, state television, much of the press and the Orthodox Church.
Sangheli, who blocked an attempt by Snegur to sack the defence minister last March, splitting the army, has said he will resign after the election "to preserve civil peace".

The president's bluff down-to-earth image generally plays well in the countryside. But the economic crisis of the past five years has fuelled support among the population of 4.3 million for the intellectual Lucinschi.
"I'm for Lucinschi," said Valya as she swept autumn leaves in front of her single-storey Chisinau house. "My pension's only 50 lei (about $10) a month and I don't always get it."
Even in the villages, conflict and poverty may take its toll on Snegur. In tiny Tintareni, most of a dozen or so voters interviewed said they wanted Lucinschi to win a four-year term.
"Snegur is to blame for the war in Dnestr and the economic problems," said one man. "Lucinschi will make things better."
There is no shortage of Snegur loyalists, however.
"I'm for Snegur. He gave us our independence, he knows what to do," said Glavia, a Chisinau housewife in her 40s. "The problem is the government don't let him to what needs to."
Snegur wants greater presidential powers to carry out reforms and dismisses the idea he wants union with Romania, from whose territory Stalin carved most of Moldova in 1940.
Lucinschi, also 56 and like the president a top communist in Soviet times, presents himself as a social democrat.

He accuses Snegur of seeking vast powers in the manner of Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko and of stirring up the Dnestr war. Playing down links with Bucharest, he reminds Moldovans they depend on Russia for their energy and much else.
